item.title: An Improved Graph Attention Network for Semantic Segmentation of Industrial Point Clouds in Automotive Battery Sealing Nail Defect Detection
item.description:
The problem

Sealing nails plug the electrolyte injection holes of automotive batteries and are laser-welded in place. Welding can leave defects such as bursts, molten beads and pinholes that compromise the battery’s safety and durability. The metal surface is highly reflective and textureless, which makes 2D imaging unreliable: it needs frequent lighting re-tuning and suffers from high false-detection rates. Traditional inspection therefore combines 2D vision to locate a defect with 3D vision to measure it, a multi-stage workflow that is complex, less efficient and accumulates errors from one stage to the next.

A 3D point cloud gives direct access to the shape of the surface, but many state-of-the-art segmentation networks, such as Point Transformer and Swin3D, rely heavily on RGB-D or intensity input. That limits their robustness when only geometry is available, which is common on reflective industrial parts. The defects themselves are also hard to learn. Defects of the same type can take very different shapes, a scan of about 100,000 points contains only about 1,000 defect points, and near a defect boundary the point coordinates barely differ from those of the surrounding surface.

How it works

LGASS (Local Graph Attention for Semantic Segmentation) segments defects directly in the 3D point cloud, so localisation and measurement happen in a single stage. It uses geometry only: the network input is each point’s surface normal, and the point coordinates determine which points are neighbours. The network is a U-Net-style encoder–decoder built around two new modules, one for attention and one for pooling.

  1. Scan the weld. A 3D laser profiler (OPT-LPC20, blue 405 nm laser stripe) scans the sealing nail at a lateral resolution of about 0.05 mm. An improved RANSAC algorithm fits the reference planes of the nail and the battery cover, and a circular region around the nail’s centre isolates the weld region for inspection.
  2. Watch the normals. Nearly every defect region shows clear changes in height and surface normal. Near a defect boundary, two adjacent points can have almost the same coordinates but clearly different normals, so the difference in normals between neighbours is a key indicator of a defect.
  3. Local Graph Attention Filter (LGAF). Each point is linked to its k nearest neighbours. For each neighbour, LGAF correlates the point’s own feature with its feature difference to that neighbour and weights the result by their spatial distance. The resulting attention weights are used to aggregate the neighbours’ features. A large normal difference produces a high attention weight, which focuses the network on defect boundaries.
  4. Spatial Attention Graph Pooling (SAG-Pooling). When the encoder downsamples, each point is scored by multiplying a learned spatial attention weight with its normal difference to a neighbour. Only the top-ranked points are kept, so points survive only if they are both spatially important and geometrically distinctive, such as those on defect edges.
  5. Label every point. The decoder uses graph-convolution blocks with positional encoding to upsample back to the full point set, with skip connections from the encoder. It assigns each point one of six classes: normal surface or one of the five defect types (burst, pit, warpage, molten bead, pinhole). A class-weighted loss gives the rarer defect classes more influence during training.

Results

mIoU (mean intersection-over-union over the classes) 79.26% and overall accuracy (OA) 99.43% on the sealing-nail dataset (mean of five runs), ahead of PTv3 (75.13% mIoU) and OA-CNN (74.04%) (Table 4).
Pinhole IoU 65.23%, against at most 60.04% for the compared methods (Table 4).
+2.59 points mIoU from LGAF and SAG-Pooling together over a baseline with standard graph convolution and pooling (Table 5).
220.9 ms to process one sample on an RTX 4070 GPU (Table 6).

The authors built a new dataset for this work from real sealing nails on inspection lines, with naturally occurring defects: 271 normal and 658 defective samples covering five defect types (170 burst, 112 pit, 132 warpage, 102 molten bead and 142 pinhole; Table 1). Code and dataset are released online. LGASS was compared with GACNet, PointNet, PointNet++, Point Transformer (PTv1 and PTv3) and OA-CNN in this geometry-only setting. Over five runs with different random seeds its mIoU stayed between 78.97% and 79.61%, and it achieved the best IoU on four of the five defect classes: pit, molten bead, warpage and pinhole.

The ablations show where the gain comes from. Replacing graph convolution with LGAF adds 2.19 points of mIoU, SAG-Pooling alone adds 0.46, and the two together add 2.59 (Table 5). Normals are the better input: in the input ablation, normals only give 79.23% mIoU, against 76.94% with coordinates only and 78.31% with both (Table 7). The class-weighted loss raises IoU on the minority classes, by 2.3 points for pinholes and 2.13 for molten beads, and lifts mIoU from 78.73% to 79.26% (Table 8). Inference needs about 2.8 GB of GPU memory. The authors note that LGASS may struggle with highly concave geometry, such as recessed nails with overlapping defects, where a fixed k-nearest-neighbour graph limits long-range context, and that rare classes such as pinholes still have lower IoU than the others.

item.title: Dynamic correlation network and structure-aware matching for robust point cloud registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that align two partially overlapping 3D scans of the same scene, for example LiDAR or RGB-D scans captured from different viewpoints. Learned methods describe each point by features aggregated from its neighbourhood and then match points across the scans. When the relative rotation between the scans is large, these features, and the correlations between them, can change with the orientation, and the matches become unstable.

The common remedy is to train with randomly rotated scans, but augmentation cannot cover the continuous space of 3D rotations, SO(3), so orientations not seen in training still degrade performance. Rotation-equivariant networks such as PARE-Net help, yet they still combine neighbouring features through a fixed multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that applies the same correlation model to every neighbourhood. And even when two superpoints (coarsely sampled points, each standing for a local patch of the scan) are correctly matched, the individual points inside them can still be paired wrongly.

How it works

The method follows the coarse-to-fine pattern: a backbone extracts coarse superpoints (a sparse set of points, each standing for a local patch of the scan) and dense point features, superpoints are matched first, and points are then matched only inside matched superpoint patches. It changes two parts of this pipeline. A Dynamic Correlation Network (DCN) inside the PAREConv-FPN backbone decides how to combine neighbouring features from rotation-invariant cues, and a Structure-Aware Point Matching (SAPM) module refines the point matches inside each patch.

  1. Rotated input. The two scans arrive at an arbitrary relative rotation; the network has to estimate the rigid transform between them even when that orientation was not seen during training.
  2. A rotation-invariant cue. For each point and its nearest neighbours, a vector-neuron encoder builds features from the relative offsets, the mean offset of the neighbourhood and their cross product. These features rotate with the scan; their magnitudes do not, so the magnitudes serve as a rotation-invariant descriptor.
  3. Dynamic kernels. A channel reallocation network turns that descriptor into softmax scores over a small bank of learnable kernels (four in the experiments), and each neighbour’s kernel is the score-weighted sum of the bank. Because the scores depend only on invariant quantities, kernel selection does not change with rotation, while the aggregated features remain rotation-equivariant.
  4. Context inside each patch. Each matched superpoint pair defines two local patches. SAPM refines every point’s descriptor with linear self-attention over its own patch, at a cost linear in the patch size; points that lie closer to a different superpoint are masked out.
  5. Consistent matches and the pose. A row-wise and a column-wise masked softmax over the patch similarity matrix are fused with per-point confidence scores. Entries that are in the top k in both directions become dense matches. Each patch yields a pose hypothesis by SVD, and a feature-based hypothesis proposer keeps the best one, without RANSAC.

Results

Registration recall (share of scan pairs aligned to an RMSE below 0.2 m) 95.4 % on 3DMatch and 79.6 % on 3DLoMatch; the 3DLoMatch result is the highest of all methods compared (Table 3).
Transformation recall (share of pairs with rotation error below 15° and translation error below 0.3 m) 82.3 % on 3DLoMatch and 82.7 % on rotated 3DLoMatch, where FCGF drops by 15.1 points relative to unrotated 3DLoMatch (Table 4).
Rotation error 0.21° on KITTI, the lowest of the compared methods, with 4.8 cm translation error and 99.8 % recall (Table 2).

3DMatch and 3DLoMatch are indoor benchmarks with overlaps above 30 % and between 10 % and 30 %; KITTI consists of outdoor driving scans. On 3DMatch the method is close to the best RANSAC-based method, BUFFER-X (95.6 %), and slightly ahead of DFAT and PARE-Net (both 94.9 %); with RANSAC in place of its own estimator it still reaches 95.2 % and 79.3 %. When arbitrary rotations are applied to 3DLoMatch, methods that rely mainly on rotation augmentation, such as FCGF and Predator, lose transformation recall, whereas methods with rotation-invariant or equivariant designs, this one included, stay stable. On KITTI, CAST has a lower translation error (2.5 cm), while this method has the lowest rotation error. In the KITTI ablation, DCN and SAPM each reduce the errors on their own, and together they lower the rotation error from 0.239° to 0.211° and the translation error from 5.5 cm to 4.8 cm (Table 6). The model has 4.04 M parameters and takes 100.29 ms on an RTX 4090, faster than CAST (129.80 ms) and PARE-Net (122.80 ms) (Table 5).

The authors note two limitations: when the overlap is critically small, coarse superpoint matches can be wrong, and highly repetitive structures can produce ambiguous descriptors that mislead hypothesis selection.

item.title: SuP: Sub-cloud Driven Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that line up two 3D scans of the same scene. Modern methods do this precisely when the two scans share a lot of geometry. In applications such as large-scale mapping and autonomous navigation, though, the views often share only a small part of the scene. Once the shared surface falls below about 30 %, classic ICP and learned methods alike struggle to find reliable correspondences, and registration slows, drifts or fails.

The paper traces these failures to the regions that are not shared: they can still be geometrically or semantically similar to each other, and matching the two whole clouds then produces wrong correspondences that obscure the correct ones. Earlier work tried to predict which points lie in the overlap, but that prediction depends on consistent features and becomes less effective on low-overlap pairs. Later methods strengthen the features with attention, geometric encodings, semantics or colour, yet their accuracy still drops as overlap falls.

How it works

SuP changes what it looks for. Two scans may overlap only a little overall, but if each is cut into smaller pieces and the pieces are matched pairwise, a subset of these sub-cloud pairs has high overlap. SuP calls these high-overlap pairs anchor pairs. It finds them in two phases, then builds its matches only from inside them.

  1. Features for the whole scan. A KPConv backbone extracts point features at several scales, and attention layers exchange context within and between the two scans. By default SuP uses the colour-enhanced backbone and attention of ColorPCR.
  2. Subdivide. Each scan is split into k sub-clouds. Farthest point sampling picks well-spread centroids, and each sub-cloud collects a centroid’s nearest neighbours within a radius.
  3. Phase I: overlap-guided prior weighting (OPS). For every source–target pair of sub-clouds, SuP measures how strongly their point features agree, counting only mutual top-ranked correlations, and keeps the best-scoring pairs as candidates. This is an efficient first filter against pairs that do not overlap.
  4. Phase II: multi-scale post-weighting (MPN). Each candidate pair is aligned with a preliminary pose from a weighted SVD. A small learned network then checks whether points that now sit close together also have similar features, at two scales. The pairs with the highest feature-consensus weights become anchor pairs. During training, the network is supervised by how well each candidate actually aligns (an alignment-aware weighting loss).
  5. Merge-to-match. Inlier correspondences from all anchor pairs are merged, refined on the denser points, and passed to a standard estimator (RANSAC or the RANSAC-free LGR) to compute the final rotation and translation.

In the reported setup, each scan is cut into 6 sub-clouds, giving 36 possible pairs. OPS keeps 24 of them, and the top 8 by feature consensus become anchor pairs.

Results

Registration recall 97.8 % on Color3DMatch and 90.2 % on Color3DLoMatch with the RANSAC-free LGR estimator, the highest among the methods compared with LGR (Table 2).
98.1 % and 90.4 % with RANSAC, and the highest registration recall at every sampling level from 5,000 down to 250 correspondences (Table 1).
Lowest pose errors: 1.374° / 0.046 m on Color3DMatch and 2.493° / 0.074 m on Color3DLoMatch (Table 3).

The evaluation uses colour-enhanced versions of the indoor 3DMatch benchmark: Color3DMatch, with pairs overlapping by more than 30 %, and Color3DLoMatch, the harder split with 10–30 % overlap. Registration recall is the share of scan pairs aligned to within 0.2 m RMSE. SuP uses ColorPCR’s colour-enhanced backbone by default; compared with ColorPCR alone, the strongest baseline, it raises recall from 96.5 % to 97.8 % on Color3DMatch and from 88.3 % to 90.2 % on Color3DLoMatch under LGR. The share of correct matches rises as well: with 250 sampled correspondences on Color3DLoMatch, 76.0 % of SuP’s matches are correct (inlier ratio), against 68.0 % for ColorPCR.

The sub-cloud step also works as an add-on to other methods. Added to GeoTransformer, it raises Color3DLoMatch recall from 74.0 % to 76.7 %; added to PEAL, from 81.2 % to 83.4 % (Table 4). In the ablation study, adding the four components one at a time (OPS, the feature-consensus weights, MPN and the alignment-aware loss) raises recall at every step on both benchmarks (Table 5). Sub-cloud size matters as well: smaller sub-clouds may lower recall because of insufficient overlap, larger ones miss local detail, and the default radius setting τ = 0.35 gives the best balance (Table 6). The paper’s limitation section notes that features from scans captured with very different sensors could weaken OPS and MPN, and suggests feature normalisation or domain adaptation as a next step.

item.title: SemReg: Semantics-Constrained Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that line up two partially overlapping 3D scans of the same scene, so that they can be merged into one. Recent learned methods describe every point by the shape around it, let the two scans exchange information through cross-attention, and then match points. Shape alone is often ambiguous, though: partial scans of a bed and a table can look geometrically alike. Cross-attention also lets every region of one scan interact with every region of the other, including pairs that are unlikely to overlap, such as a chair in one scan and a table in the other. These superfluous interactions lead to wrong matches.

Indoor scans captured with RGB-D cameras come with colour images, and semantic understanding is far more mature for 2D images than for 3D geometry. An earlier cross-modal method, PCR-CG, added image colour to the 3D features, but it uses only colour, not the semantic content of the images, and its features remain inconsistent.

How it works

SemReg is a 2D–3D cross-modal network. It keeps a standard 3D backbone for shape features and adds a semantic signal taken from the RGB frames, which it uses in three places: inside attention, at matching time, and in the training loss.

  1. Two scans with their colour frames. The input is a pair of partially overlapping point clouds, each with its RGB images. A KPConv backbone downsamples each cloud and extracts local shape features.
  2. Semantic features from the images. A pretrained DINOv2 network, kept frozen, extracts features from the RGB images. Using depth and the camera parameters, these are projected onto the 3D points and added to the shape features in self-attention.
  3. A semantic prior guides cross-attention. For each source point, SemReg finds the target points whose semantic features closely resemble its own and places a Gaussian over 3D distance around each one. The mixture of these Gaussians, the Gaussian Mixture Semantic Prior (GMSP), weights cross-attention so that features interact mainly between semantically similar regions.
  4. Matching within similar semantics. The Semantics Constrained Matching module sets the score of a candidate pair to zero when the semantic prior says the two points belong to unrelated regions. During training, a Semantics Aware Focal Loss supervises only pairs that are semantically related.
  5. Pose from the surviving matches. The final rotation and translation are estimated from the correspondences with RANSAC, and can be refined further with ICP.

Results

Registration recall 94.7 % on 3DMatch and 75.9 % on 3DLoMatch, the highest of all methods compared on both (Table 1).
95.4 % and 77.4 % after ICP refinement (Table 2).
Replacing all four semantic components (semantics constrained matching, semantics aware focal loss, semantic self-attention and GMSP-guided cross-attention) with standard counterparts drops recall to 92.1 % and 66.5 % (Table 3).

The evaluation uses 3DMatch, an indoor RGB-D benchmark, and its low-overlap split 3DLoMatch (scan pairs with 10–30 % overlap). Registration recall is the share of scan pairs whose estimated transformation is accurate to within 0.2 m (RMSE). SemReg leads on both splits, ahead of SIRA-PCR on 3DMatch and GeoTransformer on 3DLoMatch, and in the paper’s ICP-refinement comparison its margin over the next-best method grows to 1.5 and 2.9 points. The semantic components matter most when overlap is small: they account for 9.4 points of recall on 3DLoMatch, against 2.6 points on 3DMatch. In one extreme case with 12.53 % overlap, where the only shared object is a chair, the semantic prior still locates the chair in the target scan and the registration succeeds, while GeoTransformer fails.

SemReg matches at a coarse level, with 0.1K–1K correspondences per pair against 6K–7K for dense methods such as GeoTransformer. Its inlier ratio (the share of correspondences within 0.1 m under the ground-truth transformation) is therefore lower than that of some competitors, although its registration recall is higher. Results on the outdoor KITTI dataset are reported in the supplementary material. The method needs RGB images aligned with the scan, so it does not apply directly to standalone point clouds; the authors suggest rendering images from the point cloud as a future workaround.

item.title: TopFormer: Topology-Aware Transformer for Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration estimates the rotation and translation that align two partially overlapping scans. Most learned methods describe each point by its local geometry, match the descriptors, reject outliers with RANSAC and solve for the transformation. Recent Transformer-based methods work on a sparse, sub-sampled set of points and let every sparse point attend to all the others, and some add the points’ relative positions so that attention knows where each point sits.

Sub-sampling throws away fine-grained structure, though, and relative position does not help when two sparse points are close to each other in space but far apart along the surface. The paper’s example is the top of a chair next to the corner of a desk: the two points have similar local geometry because they lie in the same neighbourhood, and their relative position barely separates them because they are close in Cartesian space. Their features become ambiguous and lead to wrong matches. In the dense point cloud the difference is easy to see, since the route from one to the other along the surface is long; in the sparse points it is hard to observe.

How it works

TopFormer follows a coarse-to-fine registration pipeline and adds one ingredient: a topological structure encoding that tells the Transformer how each pair of sparse points is connected along the surface. Because the sparse points are a subset of the dense points, this surface information can be measured on the dense cloud and handed to the sparse points, which the authors call a sparse-through-dense strategy.

  1. Close in space, far along the surface. A KPConv encoder extracts local features at a sparse and a dense level. Two sparse points such as a chair top and a desk corner can look alike to it, and their relative position does little to separate them.
  2. Sparse points inside the dense graph. Down-sampling uses furthest point sampling, so every sparse point is also a dense point. On the dense points, TopFormer builds a K-nearest-neighbour graph, keeping only edges shorter than a radius τ.
  3. Geodesic distance by shortest path. For two sparse points p and q, Dijkstra’s algorithm on the dense graph gives the geodesic distance from p to q, the length of the shortest route along the surface.
  4. Direction from normals, independent of their sign. Normals estimated by PCA are unoriented, and scans can be in arbitrary poses, so the normals are hard to re-orient consistently. TopFormer therefore uses the sines of the angle between the normal at p and the vector from p to q, and of the angle between the two normals; flipping a normal turns an angle α into π − α and leaves the sine unchanged.
  5. Encoding inside attention, then matching. The geodesic distance, the Euclidean distance and the two sines are mapped by a sinusoidal function into the topological structure encoding, which is added to the keys of self-attention. Cross-attention then lets the two clouds exchange information; sparse points are matched from a confidence matrix, the matches are refined at the dense level with an optimal transport layer, and RANSAC estimates the final rotation and translation.

Results

Registration recall (share of scan pairs aligned to an RMSE below 0.2 m) of 92.4 % on 3DMatch and 75.1 % on 3DLoMatch with 5,000 correspondences, against 92.0 % and 75.0 % for GeoTransformer (Table 1).
On KITTI, 99.8 % registration recall with a relative translation error of 6.7 cm, the lowest in the comparison (Table 2).
Removing the topological structure encoding lowers recall to 89.7 % and 67.4 % on 3DMatch and 3DLoMatch (Table 3).

The indoor experiments use 3DMatch and its low-overlap split 3DLoMatch, which holds the scan pairs with 10–30 % overlap. Registration recall is the share of pairs whose estimated transformation has an RMSE below 0.2 m, computed with 50K RANSAC iterations. TopFormer’s registration recall is the highest, or tied for highest, at every correspondence number tested (5,000 down to 250) on both splits, and its feature matching recall on 3DMatch stays between 98.4 % and 98.7 %.

Its inlier ratio is below GeoTransformer’s at 5,000 correspondences (71.7 % against 71.9 % on 3DMatch, 37.2 % against 43.5 % on 3DLoMatch), but higher at smaller numbers, for example 82.8 % against 76.0 % on 3DMatch and 53.1 % against 46.2 % on 3DLoMatch at 1,000. On the outdoor KITTI odometry data, most of the compared methods already reach 99.8 % recall; TopFormer matches that, with a rotation error of 0.27°.

The ablation study shows that both parts of the encoding contribute. Without the geodesic distance, registration recall falls from 92.4 % to 90.3 % on 3DMatch and from 75.1 % to 72.3 % on 3DLoMatch; without the normal-based directional terms it falls to 91.9 % and 73.9 %. Dropping the encoding entirely, which leaves a vanilla Transformer, costs 2.7 and 7.7 points of recall, and the inlier ratio falls by 8.6 and 5.6 points.

item.title: A Point Cloud Contour Extraction Method based on Plane Segmentation
item.description:
The problem

Extracting contour features from point clouds is used in industrial inspection, robot operation and related fields. Point clouds from real devices contain noise and carry no topological relationships between points, which makes contours hard to detect. Plane detection has been approached with Hough transforms, region growing and iterative RANSAC; boundary extraction with triangular meshes, breakline sorting with B-spline fitting, and the alpha shape algorithm. Alpha shapes can extract the inner and outer contour points of polygons, but for point clouds with a large data volume its time complexity is high.

Plain RANSAC has a weak spot of its own: it tolerates obvious noise, but points just off the plane, such as those of an adjacent plane, fall within the distance threshold and introduce errors. The paper targets the contours of the surfaces of an object, here the contours of the chips on a circuit board.

How it works

The method has two stages. Plane segmentation fuses RANSAC with PCA to split the cloud into planar point sets. Contour extraction then turns each plane into a 2D image, finds its boundary from the image gradient, and maps the boundary points back into 3D space.

  1. RANSAC proposes planes. Three far-apart points are drawn at random and a plane is fitted through them; points within a distance threshold dth of the plane join its set. After Niterate iterations the largest set is kept as the current plane and removed from the cloud, and the search repeats until fewer than Nminnum points remain.
  2. PCA refines and cleans the planes. Each set is refitted by PCA: the plane passes through the centroid, and its normal is the eigenvector of the covariance matrix with the smallest eigenvalue. Two planes whose normals differ by less than 15° are merged if more than 90% of their points lie within dth of the other plane; plane pairs with too few points are removed. This repeats until no plane can be merged or removed.
  3. Flatten each plane into an image. A rotation matrix turns the planar point cloud parallel to the XOY plane, and a projection with focal lengths and offsets maps it into a 2D image. Pixels holding object points are set to 0, all others to 1.
  4. Find the boundary from gradients. The image is smoothed with a Gaussian filter, and the gradient magnitude and direction are computed. A preliminary edge pixel is kept as a boundary point only if its value is the largest among its neighbours along the gradient direction.
  5. Map back to 3D. The boundary pixels are transformed back through the projection and the inverse rotation, giving the contour points in 3D space.

Results

Contour of one chip in 64.614 ms, against 745.253 ms for alpha shapes, on the same 62,668-point cloud (Table 1).
919 boundary points (a denser, continuous outline) found by the proposed method, against 514 for alpha shapes (a sparse, broken outline) (Table 1).

The experiments extract the contours of the chips on a circuit board, running on an Intel i7-12700 CPU with 16 GB of memory. For plane segmentation, the method is compared with region growing and conventional RANSAC on the same data. On the chip shown below, region growing also takes in a neighbouring region and RANSAC a strip attached below the chip, whereas PCA-RANSAC returns the chip surface alone; the paper describes its result as the one least affected by noise.

For boundary extraction the method is compared with the alpha shape algorithm. On a single chip, alpha shapes returns a sparse, broken outline, while the proposed method returns a denser, continuous one in less time.

item.title: Gap measurement method based on projection lines and convex analysis of 3D point clouds
item.description:
The problem

The gap between the lower surface of a relay and the ground (the base the relay stands on) is a critical factor in relay quality: it affects the relay’s conductivity and reliability, and for a qualified relay it must be less than 0.07 mm in the working state. Common displacement sensors each have drawbacks: eddy-current sensors must be customised to the measured part and are relatively costly, inductive sensors are disturbed by temperature, humidity and electromagnetic interference, capacitive sensors need a high-voltage supply and have large nonlinear error, and photoelectric sensors cope poorly with ambient light.

Optical measurement avoids contact, but each kind has a limit. Two earlier vision methods for measuring levitation gaps, Pixel Area and SelfConvNet, trade speed against accuracy: Pixel Area is fast but less accurate, SelfConvNet more accurate but slow. 2D methods also lose depth, including in occluded areas, which limits their accuracy. 3D point clouds keep that information, but their disorder and sparsity make the measurement time-consuming. On top of this, metal surfaces are prone to defects such as pits and burrs because of the limits of machining.

How it works

The method combines two measurement models. A 2D projection-line model measures the gap from a backlit image of it; a 3D surface point-cloud model locates the support surface between the relay and the ground and measures the gap against it. In inspection, the fast 2D model runs first and the 3D model checks the relays that pass.

  1. Backlit projection image. A highly directional backlight shines through the gap; it suppresses the diffraction of the illuminating light so that the edges image clearly. The camera sees the relay’s lower edge l0 and the base edge l1 as two clear straight lines with a bright gap between them.
  2. Projection lines. After guided filtering, which smooths noise while preserving edges, vertical search lines cross the region of interest, and on each line the two points with the largest Sobel gradient mark the edges. A line-deviation index discards points that differ from both neighbours by more than a threshold, which removes the noise points caused by burrs. Least-squares lines are fitted to the remaining points, and the pixel distance d between them is converted to millimetres with D = k·d, where the coefficient k is averaged over measurements of known gaps.
  3. Point-cloud clean-up. A line-laser profiler captures the relay’s lower surface as a 3D point cloud. A point is treated as an outlier when too many of its neighbours lie farther than a distance threshold. Connected-component segmentation then splits the surface into separate regions.
  4. Convex hull and centroid. Fitting a surface to the point cloud is complex, and its efficiency and accuracy are hard to guarantee together. Instead, the method builds the convex hull of the surface points with a fast convex-hull algorithm and computes the relay’s centroid, weighting each material part by its density. An object comes to rest when the resultant force and moment on it are zero, so the hull face that the centroid, projected along gravity, falls on is the support surface. The gap is the vertical distance from the points of the lower surface to this plane.
  5. Two-stage inspection. The projection-line model is the coarse stage and screens every relay. Relays that pass go to the point-cloud model, the fine stage, for a second measurement.

Results

Combined 2D + 3D model: average error 0.0054 mm, maximum error 0.009 mm on gaps of 0–0.1 mm, the lowest of the five models compared (Pixel Area, SelfConvNet, projection-line, point-cloud and combined; Fig. 17).
Misjudgement (false-drop) rate 0.05% at 182.4 ms per relay for the combined model on 11,931 relays, against 2% at 236.8 ms for the point-cloud model alone and 5% at 19.8 ms for the projection-line model alone (Table 2).
Average error 0.0087 mm for the point-cloud model and 0.016 mm for the projection-line model (Fig. 17).

The experiments use a 4000 × 3000 camera with a highly directional backlight for the 2D images and an OPT-LPE50 3D laser profiler for the point clouds. The models are compared with Pixel Area and SelfConvNet. For accuracy, gaps from 0 to 0.1 mm at equal steps were set on a single relay. Pixel Area had the largest errors (maximum 0.047 mm, average 0.038 mm), followed by the projection-line model (0.021 and 0.016 mm), SelfConvNet (0.02 and 0.0095 mm) and the point-cloud model (0.015 and 0.0087 mm). In the linearity test, the point-cloud model followed the true gap more closely than Pixel Area and SelfConvNet, and the combined model was the most linear.

In the factory inspection test, 11,931 relays were measured, 9,247 good and 2,684 defective. The projection-line model was both more accurate and faster than Pixel Area (6.6%, 48.5 ms), and the point-cloud model beat SelfConvNet (2.6%, 510 ms) on both counts. The combined model had the lowest false-drop rate (the share of relays misjudged) and was faster than both the point-cloud model and SelfConvNet, meeting the requirements of real-time on-site inspection. Manual inspection of mis-detected relays showed surface defects of varying degree, particularly pits and burrs. At a pit, edge occlusion makes the projection image show the lower surface at line b rather than at the pit bottom, line a, so Pixel Area, SelfConvNet and the projection-line model, which all work from projection images, lose accuracy there. The point-cloud model measures the distance between the entire surface and the support surface, which makes it less susceptible to pits. The authors sum up the trade-off: 2D methods are simple and fast but limited by the missing dimension and more prone to errors from surface defects, while 3D methods are more accurate and reliable at the cost of longer processing time.

item.title: Weighted Point Cloud Normal Estimation
item.description:
The problem

Raw point clouds from scanners carry no normals and are often corrupted by noise, yet accurate normals help downstream tasks such as noise filtering and surface reconstruction. The classic approach, PCA, computes each point’s normal from the covariance of its neighbours; it is simple but tends to blur details and is fragile on noisy data. Learning-based regressors such as PCPNet and Nesti-Net are more robust to noise, but they ignore that neighbouring points contribute differently to the central point’s normal, which can make them inaccurate on complex surfaces. Surface-fitting methods such as DeepFit and AdaFit adapt well to complicated geometry but become less robust under severe noise.

How it works

The method regresses the normal of each point from a local patch around it, and it learns to weight the points of that patch by how relevant they are to the central point. Training has two stages: a contrastive pre-training stage that teaches the point encoder and weight regressor to relate patches to normals, and a normal estimation stage that fine-tunes them together with a normal regressor.

  1. A local patch. For each point, the patch contains its N nearest neighbours (N = 700 in the experiments). The patch is normalised to a unit sphere and aligned with a rotation R computed by PCA on the patch.
  2. Uniform weights fall short. Regressing the normal with every point weighted equally lets less relevant neighbours pull the estimate away from the true normal.
  3. Learned point weights. A point encoder built from DGCNN’s EdgeConv layers produces per-point features, and an MLP weight regressor predicts a weight for each point. The training target is the squared cosine between the central point’s ground-truth normal and each neighbour’s ground-truth normal, so points with similar normals count as more relevant. The weights multiply the features element-wise, F′ = W ⊙ F.
  4. Contrastive pre-training. A second branch encodes the central point’s ground-truth normal with MLPs. Both features pass through projection heads, and a temperature-scaled cross-entropy loss pulls each patch–normal pair together while pushing apart the other pairs in the batch. The weight loss is added to this loss.
  5. Weighted normal regression. The pre-trained encoder and weight regressor are fine-tuned with a normal regressor of fully connected layers, trained with a cosine loss plus the weight loss. The predicted normal is normalised and rotated back with R⁻¹.

Results

Average normal-angle RMSE 17.42° over the four noise levels of the PCPNet shapes with Gaussian noise, the lowest of all compared methods (AdaFit 17.66°, DeepFit 18.14°, best PCA setting 20.23°) (Table I).
Lowest error at the 0.60 %, 0.84 % and 1.20 % noise levels (noise as a share of the bounding-box diagonal), e.g. 21.48° vs 21.94° for AdaFit at 1.20 % (Table I).
On the PCPNet validation set, the full pipeline reaches 14.46°, against 21.15° for the baseline trained with the cosine loss alone (Table II).

The synthetic test set contains 19 PCPNet shapes, each with four Gaussian noise levels (0.36 %, 0.6 %, 0.84 % and 1.2 % of the bounding-box diagonal); the method is compared with PCA, the surface-fitting methods DI (Deep Iterative), DeepFit and AdaFit, and the regression methods PCPNet and Nesti-Net. At the lowest noise level DeepFit is slightly ahead (13.18° vs 13.25°); the method’s advantage appears as the noise grows. The ablation shows that both ideas matter: without the weight regression the error is 14.70°, and without the contrastive pre-training it is 18.21°.

On raw scans from the Kinect Fusion dataset, compared against the clean normals the dataset provides, the method has lower error than AdaFit and Nesti-Net on the three shapes shown. On the Paris-rue-Madame street scans, where no ground truth exists, its normals are tidier on complex areas such as a window lattice while keeping features such as a building eave and a car light. Used as input to point cloud filtering, its normals give the best filtering result by Chamfer distance, and in Poisson reconstruction of a sharp Star shape they give a more accurate tip.

item.title: Random screening-based feature aggregation for point cloud denoising
item.description:
The problem

Point clouds captured by sensing devices are contaminated by noise from the environment and the limited precision of the devices, which corrupts the geometry they describe. Traditional optimisation-based denoising needs careful parameter tuning and can struggle to remove noise and preserve features at the same time. Learning-based methods ease the tuning, but they are usually trained on data with uniform point distributions and densities, and they become less robust when the noise is severe or the point density varies.

A common way to fully exploit point position information is to fuse the features of larger patches into smaller sub-patches. That technique is typically used when the training data has a uniform point resolution, which can make the network less robust on points with varying sampling density. This paper instead screens points at random and fuses the denser patch’s global feature into the remaining points.

How it works

The network denoises each point from its local patch. An encoder extracts point features; two random screening-based feature aggregation modules then each drop half of the points at random and fuse the global feature of the denser patch (the patch before screening) into the half of the points that remain. Finally, point-wise weights decide how much each remaining point contributes to the displacement that moves the noisy point towards the clean surface.

  1. Build a local patch. For each noisy point, the neighbours within a ball of radius r (5 % of the bounding-box diagonal) form a patch. The patch is translated to the origin, scaled to a unit sphere, rotated into a canonical pose by PCA, and padded or downsampled to N = 500 points.
  2. Encode and screen. A graph-based encoder with Dense Blocks produces an N × C feature matrix. The network extracts a global feature from it and randomly keeps half of the point features.
  3. Fuse dense into sparse. The global feature is copied N/2 times and concatenated with the features of the screened sub-patch; an MLP turns them into an N/2 × 2C matrix. The sparser sub-patch now carries richer geometric information from the denser patch.
  4. Repeat once more. The same screening and fusion run again, leaving N/4 points with 4C channels each. In the paper’s ablation, this two-stage cascade is more effective than a single aggregation layer.
  5. Weight and move. The network regresses a weight for each of the N/4 points; a weighting loss trains points closer to the tangent plane of the patch centre to receive higher weights. The weighted features are max-pooled and decoded into a displacement vector, which is added to the noisy point. Training combines this weighting loss with a surface proximity loss.

Results

Lowest average errors on the PUNet test set: Chamfer distance (CD) 2.25 and point-to-mesh distance (P2M) 0.65 (×10⁴), against 2.40 and 0.75 for MoDNet, the next best (Table 1).
CD 2.299 and P2M 0.920 on 1,792 CAD shapes from the ABC dataset, against 2.511 and 1.104 for MoDNet and 2.719 and 1.302 for Score (Table 2).
In the ablation, the full pipeline reaches P2M 0.961, against 1.149 without feature aggregation and 1.407 without the weighting loss (Table 3).

The network is trained on PUNet’s 40 training shapes, with Gaussian noise of 0.5 % to 2 % of the bounding-sphere radius added on the fly. The PUNet test set has 20 shapes at 10,000 and 50,000 points, each with 1 %, 2 % and 3 % noise; the method has the lowest Chamfer distance (CD) and point-to-mesh distance (P2M) in most of these settings and on average. On real depth-camera scans from the Kinect Fusion dataset, whose noise differs from Gaussian noise, it has the lowest P2M on all three scans shown (Fig. 4), and it also leads on the irregularly sampled icosahedron above. The Paris-rue-Madame street scans, captured by a mobile laser scanner, have no ground truth, so that comparison is visual only (Fig. 6).

Two further checks support the design. Keeping half of the features at each screening step gives the lowest P2M, 0.961, against 1.270, 1.254 and 1.251 for ratios of 1/3, 2/3 and 3/4 (Table 4). Compared with the cascaded scale feature aggregation used in earlier work, the method performs similarly at lower noise levels but preserves geometry better under severe noise (Fig. 7). The denoised point clouds can also be turned into meshes with Poisson reconstruction, where the paper shows more accurate results on edges and complicated regions (Fig. 8).

item.title: Towards uniform point distribution in feature-preserving point cloud filtering
item.description:
The problem

Raw point clouds from scanners contain noise, so they are usually filtered before upsampling, surface reconstruction or other downstream use. A good filter should move the noisy points back onto the underlying surface, keep sharp edges and corners, and leave the points evenly spread. Existing methods tend to manage only part of this. Position-based methods such as CLOP smooth well but, since they ignore normals, tend to smear sharp features. Normal-based methods keep sharp edges better, but their filtered points are often unevenly distributed, and some that include a repulsion term still leave gaps near the edges. Deep learning methods need noisy training data with ground truth and work on local patches; they too give uneven distributions, even with a repulsion loss, and sparse or unevenly sampled inputs are hard for them.

The paper builds on the edge-aware point update of an earlier low-rank filtering method. On its own, that update moves points towards sharp edges, where they concentrate and leave gaps beside the edge. These gaps hurt downstream steps such as upsampling and surface reconstruction.

How it works

The method has two phases. It first smooths the point normals, then updates the point positions using those normals. The position update minimises the sum of two terms: an edge-aware data term that approximates the noisy surface while preserving geometric features, and a repulsion term that controls the point distribution.

  1. Noisy input. The input is a noisy point cloud with normals. If it has only positions, initial normals are estimated with principal component analysis (PCA).
  2. Normal filtering. The normals are smoothed with bilateral filtering. The quality of the filtered points depends heavily on the quality of these normals.
  3. Data term. For each point and each neighbour in its local patch, the update adjusts the angles between the vector joining the two points and their normals so that the vector becomes perpendicular to both normals. This brings points onto the underlying surface and preserves sharp features, but used alone it moves points towards the edges and leaves gaps.
  4. Repulsion term. A repulsion term based on point coordinates and normals pushes neighbouring points apart perpendicular to the neighbour’s normal, with a weight that decays smoothly with distance. A parameter µ sets its strength.
  5. Iterate. Both terms are combined in one gradient-descent update per point (Eq. 6 of the paper), computed on a patch of the k nearest neighbours and repeated for t iterations. Most experiments use k = 30, µ = 0.3 and t = 5 (Table 1).

Results

Average Chamfer distance 5.80 × 10−5 on five models with synthetic noise, the lowest (lower is better) of the seven methods compared; the next best, RIMLS, averages 7.12 × 10−5 (Table 2).
Average mean square error 15.69 × 10−3, again the lowest average (Table 3).
0.91–28.16 s per model, faster than CLOP, TotalDenoising, PointCleanNet and Pointfilter on all nine models timed (Table 5).

The method is compared with a position-based method (CLOP), two normal-based methods (GPF and RIMLS) and three deep learning methods (TotalDenoising, PointCleanNet and Pointfilter, abbreviated TD, PCN and PF). The quantitative tests use five models with synthetic Gaussian noise of 0.5 % or 1.0 % (Bunnyhi, Rockerarm, Icosahedron, Dodecahedron and Kitten). The method has the lowest Chamfer distance on four of the five models and the lowest mean square error on three. On raw scans (Nefertiti, BuddhaStele, Realscan and David) there is no ground truth, so these are compared visually; the paper reports that its method keeps details such as sharp edges, the steps of BuddhaStele and facial features better than the others. The authors attribute the low errors to the more uniform point distribution: RIMLS, for example, gives comparable visual results in some cases but larger errors in most, owing to its uneven distribution. Without the repulsion term, some points concentrate at the edges.

Further tests cover point density, noise levels from 0.5 % to 3.0 %, irregular sampling, holes and an indoor scene. The authors state two limitations: as a normal-based method it depends on the quality of the input normals, and it may give less desirable results at very high noise (1.5 % is already more challenging than 0.5 % and 1.0 %). Big holes that severely disrupt the surface are also hard to fill, and the best neighbourhood size k depends strongly on point density.

item.title: Iteratively weighted principal component analysis and orientation consistency for normal estimation in point cloud
item.description:
The problem

A point cloud is only a set of 3D coordinates. Many later steps, such as denoising, segmentation, surface reconstruction and visualisation, also need a surface normal at every point, so normal estimation is a basic operation in point cloud processing. The classical method, by Hoppe et al., fits a plane to each point’s nearest neighbours with principal component analysis (PCA) and takes the plane’s normal. It assumes the neighbourhood is close to a plane, and it does not perform well where points are sparse or where the surface has sharp edges: for example, normals can turn gradually around a right angle instead of following the true edge (Fig. 2).

Where point density varies and sharp features occur, the normal directions of adjacent points can also be inconsistent, some pointing inside and some outside. Reconstruction methods such as ball-pivoting and Poisson need consistently oriented normals. Wrong normals at sharp features blur those features after reconstruction, and inconsistent orientations can break the reconstructed surface.

How it works

The method keeps PCA plane fitting as its core and adds two things around it. To make the normals more robust and reliable, it weights every neighbour by distance and by normal similarity and repeats the weighted fit a few times; the authors call this Iteratively Weighted PCA (IWPCA). To make the orientation consistent, it first flips normals using the centre of the cloud and then propagates orientation along a minimal spanning tree (MST).

  1. Local plane fit. A Kd-tree finds the k nearest neighbours of each point, and a least-squares plane is fitted to them. The normal is the eigenvector belonging to the smallest eigenvalue of the neighbourhood covariance matrix.
  2. Bilateral weights. IWPCA centres the covariance matrix on the point itself and weights each neighbour twice. The spatial weight decreases with the neighbour’s distance from the point, controlled by σd, usually half the kNN search radius. The normal weight decreases as the neighbour’s normal departs from the point’s normal, controlled by σn, usually 15° to 30°. In the first pass every point’s normal is set to (1, 0, 0), so the normal weight starts out uniform.
  3. Iterate. Each new pass uses the normals of the previous pass in the normal weight. More iterations give a better estimate but cost more time; the authors recommend 2 or 3, and the last pass is the result.
  4. Pre-flip towards the outside. The centre of the whole cloud is computed, and every normal that points towards it is flipped.
  5. Propagate along a minimal spanning tree. Prim’s algorithm builds an MST over neighbouring points, with edge weight 1 − |ni · nj|. Starting from the root, each child’s normal is flipped when its dot product with its parent’s normal is negative.

For sharp parts, the normals can additionally be smoothed with the same spatial and normal weights (bilateral weighted smoothing). In the authors’ tests this made the normals on sharp parts more robust but lowered their reliability, so they recommend it only when needed, since IWPCA already improves robustness at edges by itself.

Results

Four test models from the Stanford Computer Graphics Lab: Stanford bunny (34,835 points), cube (39,846), sharp cone (50,000) and a scanned surface (30,443), all with σn = 30° and σd = 0.5 (Table 1).
Stanford bunny runtime: 564 ms for PCA, 697 ms for one IWPCA iteration, 896 ms for three (Table 1).
2 or 3 iterations recommended (Section 4.1).
Sharper cube edges and corners in Poisson reconstruction from IWPCA normals than from classical PCA normals (Fig. 8).

The comparisons in the paper are visual. On the cube, IWPCA improves the robustness of the normals at the sharp edges, and after the MST re-orientation the reliability, robustness and orientation consistency of all normals improve and the shape of the cube is clearer (Fig. 7). When the cube is reconstructed with the Poisson method, the edges and corners obtained from IWPCA normals are sharper and clearer than those from classical PCA normals (Fig. 8). On the sharp cone, classical PCA gives unsatisfactory normals at the tip, leaves some normals uncomputed and points many bottom normals inward; IWPCA improves robustness at both the top and the bottom (Fig. 9). On the scanned surface, the pre-flip and MST propagation (steps 4–5) turn inconsistent normals so that the vast majority point to the raised side (Fig. 11).

IWPCA costs more computation than classical PCA, and its runtimes include the normal re-orientation. With one iteration it is slower than PCA; with three iterations it is somewhat faster than running classical PCA three times. The experiments ran on Windows 7 (64-bit) with an Intel Core i7-5650U CPU at 2.20 GHz and 8 GB RAM. The neighbourhood size k and the weight parameters σd and σn are hard to determine and were chosen from experience; the authors suggest deriving them from local curvature, noise distribution and point density in future work.
